result.summary: Pausanias recounts the foundation myths of Ionian cities: Colophon and Claros, Lebedus, Teos, Erythrae, Clazomenae and Phocaea. He stresses the mixing of Greeks with Carians and others, and the role of Codrus' sons as leaders.

scenes.title: Colophon and the Claros oracle
scenes.summary: Cretans under Rhacius settle Claros; Manto, a captive from Thebes, marries Rhacius and their son Mopsus expels the Carians. Later Colophon's kings and its fall to Lysimachus are noted.
scenes.stakes: Manto and her fellow captives need a home; the Carians stand to lose their land.

scenes.title: Lebedus
scenes.summary: Lebedus was emptied by Lysimachus and was once held by Carians until Andraemon drove them out.
scenes.stakes: The Carians lose their city to the Ionians.

scenes.title: Settlement of Teos
scenes.summary: Minyae from Orchomenus settle Teos, followed by Ionians under Apoecus and later settlers from Attica and Boeotia, all received kindly.

scenes.title: Erythrae's mixed founders
scenes.summary: Erythrae is founded by Cretans under Erythrus, joined by Lycians, Carians and Pamphylians, then reorganized by Cleopus.

scenes.title: Clazomenae
scenes.summary: Ionians guided by Parphorus build Scyppius, then Clazomenae, later moving to an island; Alexander later joined it to the mainland.
scenes.stakes: Fear of the Persians drives the settlers to the island.

scenes.title: Phocaea and the Codrid kings
scenes.summary: Phocians settle by agreement with Cyme and accept Codrid kings to join the Pan-Ionic confederacy.
scenes.stakes: Admission to the Ionian confederacy depends on accepting Codrid kings.

analysis.text: Ionian colonization is presented as a mixture of peoples, Greek and non-Greek, rather than a pure Athenian migration.
The accounts reflect Ionian cities' claims to descent from Codrus and mainland Greek origins, which legitimized membership in the Pan-Ionic confederacy.

fun_facts.text: Claros was excavated in the 20th century, revealing the Apollo temple and oracle complex described by ancient writers.

language_notes.text: Refers to the Epigoni's capture of Thebes, the sequel to the Seven against Thebes. Thersander, son of Polynices, led the Argives; Tiresias was the blind Theban seer.
"The god sent them to form a colony": Apollo's Delphic oracle directed the captives to found a settlement overseas, a common pattern in Greek colonization stories.
"On mutual conditions" means by agreed terms: the Ionians and Colophonian Greeks shared citizenship as equals.
"Usurped" means seized by force or without right; the kingship was taken by the sons of Codrus rather than inherited.
Refers to Pausanias' earlier account of Lysimachus, a successor of Alexander who ruled Asia Minor and forcibly moved populations to enlarge Ephesus.
Minyæ were an old Greek people of Orchomenus in Boeotia; Athamas was a legendary king there, and the text distinguishes this later descendant from the earlier Athamas.
"The former... the latter" refers back to the Attic group under Damasus and Naoclus and the Boeotian group under Geres.
Sarpedon, brother of Minos in Cretan tradition, fled Crete, and the Lycians were said to descend from his followers.
Calchas was the Greek seer at Troy (Ilium); some Greeks wandered with him after the war, supposedly founding Pamphylian settlements.
Alexander the Great joined the island to the mainland with a causeway, so it became a peninsula.
The "return of the Dorians" is the Dorian invasion of the Peloponnese, which displaced earlier peoples such as those of Cleonæ and Phlius.

context_notes.text: Claros, near Colophon, housed a famous oracle of Apollo, whose priest gave answers after drinking water from a sacred spring.
Manto was the daughter of the seer Tiresias; in tradition she became a prophetess, and her son Mopsus was a famed seer.
Codrus was the legendary last king of Athens; his sons were said to have led the Ionian migration to Asia Minor.
Carians were the pre-Greek inhabitants of southwestern Asia Minor, often displaced in Greek foundation legends.
Melanthus was the Athenian king and father of Codrus; his descendants led many Ionian migrations to Asia Minor.
Ionian cities required rulers of Codrus' royal line for admission to the Pan-Ionic league, which met for common worship and festivals.

literary_notes.text: Mopsus is presented in one stroke as a decisive founder, completing the Greek takeover that his parents began through marriage and alliance.
Promethus kills his brother, yet is brought home and buried by his victim's sons, a bitter reversal that closes the family feud.
The brief remark that Carians were "mixed up" with Greeks plainly states the mixed population of Ionian cities.
"Was destined" leaps ahead to Alexander's later engineering feat, looking forward across the historical narrative.
